assembly.name: Cooling — N493 thermal management & stack
assembly.description: Cooling & fluids per R9: coolant G13 (TL-VW 774 J), 10.0 L total — superseded by mixable G12evo; engine oil VW 502 00, 5.7 L with filter; A/C refrigerant R134a at 500 ±15 g (NOT R1234yf on this pre-facelift car), PAG oil differing by compressor brand (Sanden G 052 154 A2 75 cc vs Denso G 052 300 A2 110 cc — their N280 valves don't interchange). There is NO radiator drain screw on the Mk7: VW fills under vacuum with VAS 6096. See docs/research/R9-cooling-fluids.md.

parts.name: N493 rotary thermal-management module
parts.description: R9 RESOLUTION: the leak-prone plastic pump/thermostat unit IS the N493 module, standard on all EA888 Gen 3 (SSP 606 + erWin Rep. Gr. 19). Map-controlled coolant 85–107 °C with the wax safety thermostat only as a 113 °C fallback. Supersession 06L121111 → 06L121111P; module bolts 9 Nm. The Audi/Schaeffler rotary-slide valve module replacing a wax thermostat: valve 1 regulates oil-cooler/head/radiator flow (~80–110 °C, up to ~107 °C light-load for low friction), valve 2 couples the block in at ~145° of valve-1 rotation. Driven by one DC motor through a worm gear; 12 V / 1,000 Hz PWM control (dossier §2).
knownIssues: THE classic Gen 3 coolant weak point: the plastic housing near the hot side goes brittle and cracks/leaks, typically 60,000–90,000 miles. Aftermarket reinforced/metal housings exist (dossier §2).

parts.name: Coolant pump (balance-shaft driven)
parts.description: The balance-shaft-driven impeller side of the N493 pump/thermostat module. R9: impeller sub-unit current number 06L121012M — with an explicit vendor warning that the generic 06L121012 pump 'does not fit the Mk7 Golf R'; VIN-verify before ordering. Pulley bolt 10 Nm + 90°, RENEW — and it is a LEFT-HAND thread, the only confirmed one on the car (R9/R12).

torqueSpec.note: Pulley bolt — LEFT-HAND thread, renew (R9/R12); module bolts 9 Nm

knownIssues: Plastic housing cracks/seeps — coolant hides under the intake manifold and mimics other leaks (R9 + dossier §2).

parts.name: Radiator (high-performance)
parts.description: The R's uprated main radiator in the MQB front stack (dossier §8).

parts.name: A/C condenser
parts.description: Forward-most of the stack (dossier §8): condenser, then radiator, then intercooler.

parts.name: Auxiliary corner radiators ×2
parts.description: R9 confirms TWO corner auxiliary radiators on the DSG car: left/DSG-side 5Q0121253H, right/engine-side 5Q0121251HA.

parts.name: Twin cooling fans & shroud
parts.description: Twin electric fans on the engine side of the radiator.

parts.name: Expansion / degas tank
parts.description: Coolant expansion tank — PHOTO-MATCHED to the operator's car (2026-08-15): it sits in the OFFSIDE gutter BESIDE THE ENGINE, not out by the wheel arch — roughly level with the front of the engine, with the brake-fluid reservoir behind it toward the bulkhead and the blue screen-wash filler ahead of it. Big round screw cap with the coolant warning symbol; cold-check the level here. Cap rating ~1.4–1.6 bar unconfirmed (R9).

parts.name: Main coolant hoses & heater feed
parts.description: Top/bottom radiator hoses off the N493/pump plus the heater-core feed through the bulkhead; the gearbox-oil heat exchanger also taps this circuit via its own switching valve (dossier §2).

parts.name: Gearbox-oil heat exchanger (DQ250)
parts.description: Oil-to-coolant exchanger keeping the wet-clutch DSG's oil in its window (dossier §2 switching-valve circuit).

parts.name: A/C refrigerant lines
parts.description: High/low-side lines from the belt-driven compressor to the condenser and on to the bulkhead expansion valve (dossier §8).

parts.name: Screen-wash UPPER reservoir & filler cap
parts.description: The Mk7 washer reservoir is TWO parts, and this is the upper one — so yes, the blue cap sits directly on top of a tank and you pour straight into it. This upper reservoir lives in the offside gutter of the engine bay and feeds the much larger LOWER tank behind the right-front arch liner through a wide throat. Total system ~3.7 L on the R/S3 (VW quote ~3–6 L for cars with headlight washers).
knownIssues: The throat/joint between upper and lower tank is a leak path — it often only shows when you fill right to the brim, which is why such a leak seems to come and go.

parts.name: Screen-wash LOWER reservoir (behind RF arch liner)
parts.description: The tank that actually holds the fluid, hidden behind the RIGHT-front (offside) wheel-arch liner. Access: front wheel off, arch-liner screws out (T25 Torx) and the liner folded back — the pumps and level sender are then right in front of you. (VW's book removes the front bumper and headlight for a FULL reservoir swap; owners doing pumps/seals go through the arch.)
knownIssues: Cracks from stone strikes and from freezing when filled with plain water — a hairline crack weeps only when the tank is full.

parts.name: Windscreen & rear washer pump V59
parts.description: ONE pump (VW designation V59) feeds BOTH the windscreen and the rear screen — it has two outlets with colour-coded hoses, so note which hose goes where before pulling them off. It pushes into a rubber grommet low on the tank and pulls straight out by hand once the hoses and plug are off. THE classic leak: that grommet hardens with age and weeps.
knownIssues: Hardened/split pump grommet → slow leak that empties the bottle while parked (the number-one cause of a Mk7 washer leak).
Fitting trap: do NOT push the grommet into the tank while refitting the pump — you cannot fish it back out without dropping the whole reservoir. Wet it with washer fluid and press the pump in gently.

parts.name: Expansion tank cap (pressure cap)
parts.description: The big black screw cap on the coolant tank — it is a PRESSURE cap, not just a lid: it holds the system at roughly 1.4–1.6 bar (rating unconfirmed against a primary source, R9) which raises the coolant's boiling point. NEVER open it on a hot engine. A tired cap seal lets the system lose pressure and boil early, which reads like a much scarier fault.
knownIssues: Perished cap seal → pressure loss, coolant weeping around the neck, early boiling and phantom overheating.

parts.name: Headlight washer pump V11 (high pressure)
parts.description: Because this car has XENON headlights it also has a headlamp washer system — and that means a SECOND, high-pressure pump (V11) on the outboard face of the tank, nearest the wing, opposite the windscreen pump. Cars without headlight washers get a smaller tank and only one pump. Working headlamp washers are an MOT requirement on xenon cars.
knownIssues: Same grommet story as V59 — and because it runs at higher pressure, a tired grommet here leaks sooner and faster.
Often killed or left unplugged after front-end/bumper work — worth testing before an MOT.

parts.name: Washer fluid level sender (G33)
parts.description: Float sender in the side of the lower tank that lights the 'top up washer fluid' warning. It sits just ABOVE the windscreen pump — a useful landmark once the liner is off. Its seal is another small leak path, and a stuck float gives a false warning on a full tank. G33 is the standard VAG designation for this sender — verify against ETKA for the exact part number.
knownIssues: Perished sender seal weeps; a stuck float reports empty when the tank is full.

parts.name: Headlamp washer jets (telescopic) ×2
parts.description: Telescopic nozzles hidden in the front bumper below each headlight — they pop out under pressure when V11 runs (with the lights on), then retract. Fed from the same tank, which is why using the headlamp washers drains the bottle so quickly.
knownIssues: Seized or stuck-out nozzles and snapped covers after a bumper knock; a nozzle stuck open dribbles fluid away and looks like a tank leak (and is an MOT fail on a xenon car).
